newsitem.title: FRANCE: French rivals clash head-on in close poll race.
newsitem.headline: French rivals clash head-on in close poll race.

text.p: France's snap parliamentary election has turned into a presidential-style head-on clash between Prime Minister Alain Juppe and Socialist challenger Lionel Jospin as polls point to a close race.

Taking to the hustings for the first time since President Jacques Chirac called next month's election on Monday, the centre-right premier accused the Socialist leader of selling out to the Communists. And Jospin hit back with a personal attack on his rival.

"(Jospin) risks blocking European construction. He is ready to sell his ideas in exchange for the poor meal the Communists are preparing," Juppe told a rally in the Mediterranean port city of Marseille.
In an attempt to forge an electoral pact with the Communists, Jospin has taken a cool stand towards plans for a single European currency which the Communists object to.

Francois Leotard, leader of the junior partner in the ruling coalition, also hit out at Jospin at the Marseille rally. "Every time Mr Jospin speaks of tough capitalists we will speak of the Marxists they really are," he said.
Jospin, who picked the depressed Paris suburb of Sarcelles for his first rally, attacked Juppe as "arrogant and authoritarian".
He said he wanted the euro "but not a euro confiscated by the financial markets. We don't want an euro that would force Europe to pursue deflationary, economic stagnation policies."
The campaign beat quickened with an IPSOS poll for the weekly Le Point predicting that the government would be returned with only a wafer-thin parliamentary majority.

It said the ruling coalition would win 292 seats in the 577-member National Assembly, with the opposition Socialists taking 256, the Communists 28 and the far-right National Front one. Thirty-one percent of those questioned on Tuesday and Wednesday did not state their voting intention.

Earlier, Juppe's office confirmed that ministers had been told to hold 1998 state spending unchanged in nominal terms for the second successive year, meaning a cut of more than one percent in real terms.
But it sought to offset the impression of austerity by trumpeting signs of an economic upturn ahead of the election, likely to be dominated by the issues of unemployment, taxes and purchasing power.

"Growth is taking off again," Budget Minister Alain Lamassoure said, pointing to what he called robust industrial production figures. He said France might make more tax cuts than planned if economic growth exceeded forecasts for 1997.

A Louis Harris survey for Valeurs Actuelles magazine said most voters believed there were alternatives to the government's economic policies meant to prepare for the single European currency from 1999.

And 69 percent of those quizzed favoured a new referendum on the introduction of the euro currency. Voters narrowly approved the Maastricht treaty on European union, including the currency, in a 1992 referendum.
The Harris survey, taken before Chirac announced the election, said 50 percent thought the single currency would fail to help "a return to economic growth", while 43 percent felt it could succeed.
Seventy-three percent believed the euro would not help to reduce unemployment in major European nations, with just 20 percent saying it would.

The Socialists, who say they favour the euro but not at the price of more austerity, accused the conservatives of trying to secure re-election before imposing draconian new measures to help to qualify for the single currency.
